description: No crow trickster is attested in Maya tradition. The Maya have no sacred or trickster crow in their mythology; the great bird of the Popol Vuh is Vucub-Caquix, the Principal Bird Deity who appears as a macaw and is defeated by the Hero Twins. The Canada country tag and the Maya-diaspora framing reflect a modern invention, not recorded tradition.
source: Popol Vuh (Christenson trans.); Maya mythology scholarship
research_notes: Maya are a Mesoamerican people (Mexico/Guatemala), not of Canada. No crow figure exists in Maya lore; the principal bird of the Popol Vuh is Vucub-Caquix, a macaw. Matches B14 precedent (crow-maya to Vucub-Caquix). Template-generated trickster.

description: Changing Woman (Asdzą́ą́ Nádleehé), also called White Shell Woman, is the central deity of Navajo religion. Born from the darkness, she lives in the west beside the ocean, aging and renewing herself with the seasons, and she bore the Hero Twins, Monster Slayer and Child of the Water, fathered by the Sun. She gave the Navajo their clans and the Blessingway ceremonies.
source: Tony Hillerman Portal, University of New Mexico (ehillerman.unm.edu); Wikipedia 'Asdzą́ą́ Nádleehé'
research_notes: Verified via the Tony Hillerman Portal and Wikipedia. Asdzą́ą́ Nádleehé is the most important Navajo deity, mother of the Hero Twins, creator of the Navajo, and central to the Blessingway. Country United States is correct.

description: Áłtsé Hashké, 'First Angry' or 'First Scolder,' is the primeval Coyote of Navajo tradition. In the origin narratives he was the first coyote made in the Third World and the first to grow angry, angering the chiefs and so bringing anger and discord among the people, foreshadowing the disorder the trickster coyote would later spread through the world.
source: Washington Matthews, Navaho Legends (1897); ehillerman.unm.edu
research_notes: Verified via Washington Matthews's Navaho Legends and the Tony Hillerman Portal. Áłtsé Hashké (First Angry / First Scolder) is the first coyote who introduced anger and strife into the world. Country United States is correct.

description: Corn Girl is a Navajo Holy Person associated with the sacred mountain Tsoodził (Mount Taylor), the southern boundary mountain of the Navajo world set with turquoise and female rain. She dwells there with Turquoise Boy, guarding corn and its growth, and stands with them as an emblem of fertility and the Navajo corn-growing cycle.
source: Navajo creation accounts (thelongbrownpath.com); Navajo ethnography
research_notes: Corn Girl is among the Navajo Holy People who dwell at Tsoodził (Mount Taylor) with Turquoise Boy, per the creation-account summary in the input and corroborating Navajo sources. Country United States is correct.

description: The Corn Maidens are the sacred corn spirits of the Pueblo peoples, especially the Zuni and Hopi, who embody the growth and life of maize. In origin accounts the maidens brought corn up from the underworld, sang and danced it into being, and when they were neglected the harvest withered until the people and their kachina priests called the maidens back.
source: World History Encyclopedia (Paiyatuma); Bunzel, Zuni origin myths
research_notes: The Corn Maidens tradition is strongest among the Zuni (seven sisters with Paiyatuma) and Hopi; the Pueblo tag is valid. The Zuni seven-maidens variant is detailed in its own slug. Country United States is correct.

description: Cyclone is a primordial wind spirit in Jicarilla Apache creation accounts, present in the darkness before the world was lit. Cyclone spied on the Hactcin, the ancestral spirits, and told Holy Boy that White Hactcin held the sun; with that knowledge Holy Boy obtained the sun and the moon, and daylight came into being.
source: UTRGV Borderlands reader, Jicarilla Apache creation (1930s oral tradition)
research_notes: Verified via the Jicarilla Apache creation account in the UTRGV Borderlands reader. Cyclone told Holy Boy about White Hactcin's sun, enabling the making of daylight. Country United States is correct.

description: Child of the Water is the Apache culture hero, one of the twins born to White-painted Woman. With his brother Killer of Enemies he rid the world of monsters, slaying the Owl-Man Giant, the Buffalo Monster, and the Eagle Monster, and he remains the model of the Apache warrior, told of across the Chiricahua and other Apache oral traditions.
source: sageventure.com, 'The Slaying of the Monsters' (Apache origin accounts)
research_notes: Verified via Apache accounts of the slaying of the monsters. Child of the Water is the son of White-painted Woman and twin brother of Killer of Enemies. Note: the input's appearance text wrongly described the Gahe Mountain Spirits; corrected here. Country United States is correct.

description: White-painted Woman, the Apache counterpart of Changing Woman, is the mother of the hero twins Child of the Water and Killer of Enemies, whom she bore on White Mountain. She is the ideal of Apache womanhood and the model for the girls' puberty ceremony, which re-enacts her power to age and then grow young again with the seasons.
source: Mescalero Apache Tribe cultural materials (mescaleroapachetribe.com)
research_notes: Verified via Mescalero Apache cultural materials. White-painted Woman is the Apache Changing Woman and the basis of the puberty rite. The input's appearance text wrongly described the Gahe; corrected to White-painted Woman. Country United States is correct.

description: The Zuni Corn Maidens are seven sisters who personify the different colors of corn, fostered and guarded by Paiyatuma, the God of Dew and Dawn and flute-playing patron of spring. When they left the Zuni in anger the harvest withered, and Paiyatuma with the Kachina Fathers brought them home with magic wands and flute songs, restoring the crops.
source: World History Encyclopedia (Paiyatuma, Joshua J. Mark, 2025); Cushing and Bunzel, Zuni origin myths
research_notes: Verified via the World History Encyclopedia article on Paiyatuma and Zuni origin myths (Cushing, Bunzel). Seven Corn Maidens fostered by Paiyatuma; their return restores the corn. Country United States (Zuni, New Mexico) is correct.

description: Corn Woman is the corn-giving spirit of the Muscogee (Creek) people, honored at the busk, the Green Corn Ceremony that begins the Creek new year. In origin accounts corn was a gift that came through a woman, and the ceremony renews the world with new fire, thanksgiving, and the first fruits of the harvest.
source: tribalcollegejournal.org (Muscogee corn tradition); Swanton, Creek mythology
research_notes: Corn Woman / Corn Mother tradition documented for the Muscogee (Creek); the Green Corn busk is the central ritual. Country United States is correct. The figure parallels Cherokee Selu.

description: Chufi, the Rabbit, is the trickster of the Muscogee (Creek) people, a small, quick animal whose cleverness and mischief animate many Creek stories. In one well-known tale he stole fire from those who kept it hidden and brought it to the people; in others he outwits larger animals, and his escapades teach the limits of cunning.
source: native-languages.org Creek legends; Alexander Posey, Chinnubbie and the Owl (Muscogee Creek stories)
research_notes: Verified via native-languages.org and Alexander Posey's Chinnubbie and the Owl. Chufi is the Creek rabbit trickster, a fire-bringer in some tales. Country United States is correct.

description: Chukfi (Chokfi), the Rabbit, is the trickster of the Chickasaw people. Clever, mischievous, and sometimes selfish, he uses his wits to outsmart larger animals and to explain how things came to be; stories tell why Rabbit has a short tail, why the possum's tail is bare, and how deer gained their antlers.
source: native-languages.org Chickasaw legends
research_notes: Verified via native-languages.org Chickasaw legends. Chukfi is the Chickasaw rabbit trickster whose tales explain the rabbit's short tail, the possum's bare tail, and the deer's antlers. Country United States is correct.

description: Ogopogo is the lake monster of Okanagan Lake in British Columbia, rooted in Syilx (Okanagan) oral tradition, where the being is called n̓x̌aʔx̌ʔitkʷ, the sacred water creature said to demand safe passage of travellers. The name 'Ogopogo' is a 1920s coinage, but the Syilx accounts of a serpentine lake spirit long predate the English nickname.
source: learn.syilx.org; tourismkelowna.com Okanagan history
research_notes: Verified via Syilx cultural sources and Okanagan histories. The Syilx name n̓x̌aʔx̌ʔitkʷ (sacred water being) predates the 1920s nickname Ogopogo. The lake tradition is chiefly Syilx (Okanagan). Country Canada is correct.

description: No owl ancestor-spirit exists in Khmer (Cambodian) tradition, and the Khmer are a Southeast Asian people, not of the United States. Cambodian folklore does regard the owl as an ill omen whose cry foretells death, but no ancestor-spirit, water spirit, or guardian owl is recorded. The entry is a template-generated invention with the wrong country and the wrong people.
source: Khmer folklore studies; no attestation
research_notes: Misattribution: the Khmer are Cambodian, not Native American, so the USA tag is erroneous. Cambodian lore treats the owl as a death-omen bird, but no owl ancestor-spirit figure exists. Parallel to other batch misassignments (owlnaturespiritsan-canada, owldeityguarani-usa).

description: Among the Muscogee (Creek), owls were regarded as vessels for the spirits of the dead: great horned owls and screech owls were thought to be embodied ghosts, restless spirits, or wizards in bird form, and an owl's cry was an omen of death. This is the closest Creek tradition to an owl ancestor-spirit, though no named guardian owl is recorded.
source: Swanton, Creek mythology; accessgenealogy.com (Creek spiritual beliefs)
research_notes: Creek tradition holds that owls embody spirits of the dead and that wizards transform into great horned owls; screech-owl calls portend death. No named ancestor-spirit guardian exists; the slug's guardian framing is reframed to the documented belief. Country United States is correct.

description: The Navajo regard the owl as a being of the spirit world tied to death: its hoot is an omen, a dream of an owl foretells death, and owls are linked to witches and to the dead. The most fearsome were 'Those That Kill With Their Eyes' (Binaa' yee aghaanii), monsters slain by the Hero Twins. No guardian ancestor-spirit owl is recorded.
source: Kluckhohn, Navaho Witchcraft (1944); University of Utah Navajo text collection
research_notes: Navajo owl traditions are genuine but are death-omen and witchcraft beliefs, not the benevolent guardian ancestor-spirit the slug implies; reframed accordingly. Country United States is correct.

description: The owl holds a place in Haida oral tradition as a crest and spirit being. In the Haida story of Kwel-Kwel the girl married the owl and their children founded the Owl crest; elsewhere the owl appears as a messenger whose cry is an omen, and shamans' familiar spirits could take owl form. It is a spirit animal rather than a forest guardian.
source: Swanton, Haida Texts and Myths (1905), 'Kwel-Kwel'
research_notes: Verified via Swanton's Haida Texts and Myths: the girl who married the Owl founds the Owl crest; owls also carry death-omen and shamanic-spirit associations. The input's 'forest guardian' framing is not attested and was reframed. Country Canada is correct.

description: No owl deity exists in Guarani religion, and the Guarani are a South American people of Paraguay, Brazil, and Argentina, not of the United States. Guarani and Paraguayan folklore instead cast the great horned owl (ñacurutú) as an evil bird of ill omen and the urutau as a spirit bird; no owl is worshipped or made a god.
source: Paraguayan and Guarani folklore studies; no attestation
research_notes: Double misattribution: the Guarani are not a North American people (USA is wrong), and no owl deity is attested in Guarani lore. The real tradition treats the great horned owl (ñacurutú) as an evil-omen bird. Parallel to earlier Guarani misassignments in the batch series.

description: No owl deity is attested in Blackfoot religion. The Blackfoot (Siksika, Kainai, Piikani) instead held that owls could be inhabited by the spirits of medicine men, and owl feathers marked warriors and leaders, as in the black-dog society leader's owl-feather bonnet. The owl is a medicine bird, never a god.
source: Wissler, Societies and Dance Associations of the Blackfoot Indians; New World Encyclopedia
research_notes: No Blackfoot owl deity exists. Real beliefs: owls inhabited by medicine-men spirits (Wissler) and owl-feather bonnets in warrior societies. The 'deity' and 'river guardian' framings are template artifacts. Country United States is correct.

description: No owl deity is attested among the Blackfoot of Canada (Siksika, Kainai, Piikani of the Blackfoot Confederacy). Their genuine owl traditions are the Owl Dance, a social and courtship dance, and the belief that owls may carry the spirits of medicine men. The owl is honored in song and story but is not a deity.
source: Blackfoot Confederacy cultural materials; Wissler, Blackfoot societies
research_notes: Canadian variant of the same finding: the Blackfoot of Alberta have no owl deity. The real traditions are the social Owl Dance and the medicine-man-spirit owl belief. Country Canada is correct for the Siksika/Kainai/Piikani.

description: No owl deity is recorded in Mi'kmaq tradition. The Mi'kmaq know the owl as kokokwes, a name drawn from the barred owl's calling, and in the celestial story of the stars the Owl is one of the hunters who pursues the Great Bear across the night sky. But the owl is never a god.
source: Rand, Legends of the Micmacs; Mi'kmaq star-lore
research_notes: No Mi'kmaq owl deity. The owl (kokokwes) appears as a celestial star-hunter and its name derives from the barred owl's call. The 'deity' and 'mountain/water spirit' framings are template artifacts. Country Canada is correct.

description: No owl ghost is attested in Mi'kmaq folklore. The documented owl traditions of the Mi'kmaq are the celestial Owl, one of the star-hunters chasing the Great Bear, and the name kokokwes for the owl. Owls are not portrayed as ghosts or water spirits in Mi'kmaq stories; the entry is a template-generated invention.
source: Rand, Legends of the Micmacs; Mi'kmaq star-lore
research_notes: No owl ghost in Mi'kmaq tradition. The closest genuine material is the celestial Owl star-hunter and the name kokokwes. The 'ghost' and 'sky guardian' framing is invented. Country Canada is correct.

description: No owl giant exists in Tlingit tradition. The documented Tlingit owl figure comes from the story of the Kîksa'dî woman who was turned into an owl after mistreating her mother-in-law; her owl cry thereafter warns of bad weather and bad news. The owl is a transformed woman and omen-bird, never a giant.
source: Swanton, Tlingit Myths and Texts (1909), 'The Kîksa'dî Woman Who Was Turned into an Owl'
research_notes: No Tlingit owl giant. The real figure is the Kîksa'dî woman transformed into an owl (Swanton). The 'giant' and 'river guardian' framing is template-generated. Country United States is valid for the Tlingit of Alaska.

description: No owl giant is attested in Tlingit tradition. The Tlingit of southeastern Alaska and British Columbia tell instead of the woman of the Kîksa'dî clan who became an owl as punishment for cruelty to her mother-in-law; her call foretells bad weather and bad news. The owl is a transformed ancestor figure, not a giant.
source: Swanton, Tlingit Myths and Texts (1909)
research_notes: Same finding as the US variant: no Tlingit owl giant. The genuine story is the Kîksa'dî owl-woman (Swanton). Tlingit territory spans Alaska and Canada; the split slug is a dataset artifact.

description: No owl giant appears in Yurok folklore. Yurok traditional narratives collected by Kroeber and others center on figures such as the Bear and her fawns, the theft of fire, and the origin of salmon; owls play no giant or guardian role. The entry is a template invention with no basis in Yurok tradition.
source: Kroeber, Yurok Myths (1976); Yurok traditional narratives
research_notes: No attestation in Yurok sources (Kroeber 1976, Yurok traditional narratives). No owl giant or owl spirit figure. The 'forest giant' framing is invented. Country United States is correct for the Yurok of California.

description: No owl guardian spirit is attested in Tlingit tradition. The Tlingit tell of the Kîksa'dî woman turned into an owl whose cry announces bad weather and bad news; elsewhere owls are linked to death omens and shamanic spirits. None of this amounts to a guardian owl, and the river-guardian framing is a template artifact.
source: Swanton, Tlingit Myths and Texts (1909)
research_notes: No Tlingit owl guardian. Real material is the Kîksa'dî owl-woman story and owl death-omen associations (Swanton). The 'guardian' and 'divine duty' framing is invented. Country United States is valid for the Tlingit of Alaska.

description: No owl guardian is attested in Tlingit tradition. Tlingit lore records the woman of the Kîksa'dî clan who was turned into an owl, whose cry warns of storms and ill news, and owls carry associations with death omens. These are the extent of Tlingit owl beliefs; no guardian or tutelary owl exists.
source: Swanton, Tlingit Myths and Texts (1909)
research_notes: Same finding as the US variant: no Tlingit owl guardian. The documented tradition is the Kîksa'dî owl-woman and owl death omens (Swanton). Country Canada is valid for the Tlingit of British Columbia.

description: No owl nature-spirit exists in San (Bushmen) tradition, and the San are an indigenous people of southern Africa, not of Canada. San mythology centers on |Kaggen, the praying-mantis trickster and creator. The entry pairs an African people with a Canadian country tag and invents an owl lake-spirit that no tradition records.
source: San mythology studies; no attestation
research_notes: Misattribution: the San (Bushmen) are of southern Africa; the Canada tag is erroneous, matching the earlier B17 San misassignment. No owl nature-spirit in San lore; |Kaggen the mantis is the central figure. Template-generated.

description: In Haida tradition the owl is bound up with the spirit world: its call is read as an omen, often of death, and in the story of Kwel-Kwel a girl's marriage to the owl founds the Owl crest of her descendants. As a night-flying spirit being it belongs to the unseen realm, though no generic nature-spirit guardian is recorded.
source: Swanton, Haida Texts and Myths (1905)
research_notes: Reframed from the invented 'nature-spirit guardian of caves' to the documented Haida owl as omen-spirit and crest figure (Swanton, Kwel-Kwel). Distinct emphasis from owl-animal-spirit-of-haida. Country Canada is correct.

description: Among the Maliseet-Passamaquoddy (Wabanaki) of the Northeast, the owl appears in story as a being of power: in the legend of the Owl Husband a girl marries the great horned owl, and owl figures also take part in Wabanaki tales. The owl is a story-being and omen, though not the forest nature-spirit guardian the entry claims.
source: Wabanaki legends (the Owl Husband); Maliseet-Passamaquoddy oral tradition
research_notes: The Owl Husband legend is shared among the Maliseet and Passamaquoddy (Wabanaki) people. Reframed from the template's invented 'springs guardian' to the documented owl lore. Country Canada is correct for the Maliseet of New Brunswick.

description: The Cheyenne hold that owls are spirits of the night: they said only the short-eared owl is a true bird, while all other owls are mista, night spirits, often of a dangerous or deathly kind. Warriors nonetheless wore owl feathers on shields and arms for night vision, and the Contraries society used owl feathers in its regalia.
source: Cheyenne tradition (powwows.com); Center of the West, Native Americans and Owls
research_notes: Verified: the Cheyenne view most owls as mista 'night spirits,' only the short-eared owl being a real bird; owl feathers were worn by warriors and the Contraries (Hohnuhke). The 'forest spirit/cave' framing was reframed. Country United States is correct.

description: The Cheyenne recognize owls as night spirits: in their belief only the short-eared owl is a genuine bird, while the other owls are mista, spirits of the night, feared as omens. Owl feathers nonetheless carried protective power, worn by warriors to see in the dark. The same belief holds wherever Cheyenne tradition is told.
source: Cheyenne tradition; Center of the West, Native Americans and Owls
research_notes: Same belief as the US variant. Note: the Cheyenne are a Plains people (Montana, Oklahoma); the Canada country tag is inaccurate, an artifact of the batch's country-split slugs. The owl-as-night-spirit tradition itself is genuine.

description: The Mi'kmaq know the owl as kokokwes, a name drawn from the barred owl's calling, and place the Owl among the celestial hunters of star-lore: in the Mi'kmaq story of the Great Bear, the Owl is one of the seven hunters who pursue the bear around the northern sky, explaining the turning of the stars.
source: Rand, Legends of the Micmacs; Mi'kmaq star-lore
research_notes: The Mi'kmaq owl is attested as a celestial star-hunter in Mi'kmaq star-lore and in the name kokokwes (from the barred owl's call). The 'water-spirit/lake guardian' framing was reframed to the genuine celestial tradition. Country Canada is correct.

description: No owl trickster exists in Cherokee folklore. In Mooney's Myths of the Cherokee the owls appear in 'The Bird Tribes' as embodied ghosts and disguised witches, the dusky horned owl being called tskïlï, 'witch,' with their cries read as omens of death. Cherokee trickster roles belong to Rabbit and Possum, not the owl.
source: Mooney, Myths of the Cherokee (1900), 'The Bird Tribes'
research_notes: Cherokee owls are witch and death-omen birds (tskïlï 'witch,' u'guku' hooting owl), not tricksters. Cherokee trickster figures are Rabbit and Possum. The 'trickster' and 'lake guardian' framing is wrong. Country United States is correct.

description: The Ocean-Spider is a monstrous water creature of Greenlandic Inuit tradition recorded by Hinrich Rink. A kayaker in the firth of Godthaab once found the bottom close beneath him where no shoal was known, remembered the elders' warnings of the ocean-spider, and barely escaped when two monstrous eyes and a gaping mouth opened beside his kayak.
source: Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), 'The Ocean-Spider'
research_notes: Verified via Rink's Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (sacred-texts tte2-147). The story is set in the firth of Godthaab (Nuuk). Related to the Inuit aasivarluut, the giant water-spider of Arctic bays. Country Greenland is correct.
